The papers of William Alexander Aldred

The Bounce Frame — The Two Results · November 6, 2026

The singularity never forms. In the bounce frame, the density caps at the Aldred Limit (ρA = 9.7×1054 g/cm³); at half the cap the null energy condition reverses, collapse halts, and the universe bounces. The vacuum catastrophe dissolves. The 10122 gap is what unregulated summation produces; bounded by the same cap, the vacuum sum saturates at the Limit and the catastrophe never arises — and the frame’s construction lands within a factor of 6.0 of the measured vacuum density. Producing the exact measured count is the program’s stated open frontier. Six manuscripts from this program are before the editors of Gravitation and Cosmology: five in peer review; the vacuum paper's reframed version has been submitted to the journal in place of the first version. The Dissolution — the full feature → · What Google’s own AI said →

Eight hundred ninety-nine papers written — the first twenty-eight of them in the 37 days between September 20 and October 27, 2026 — by a man with no backing, no engineers, and no team, working from a laptop. Nine hundred one are publicly deposited on Zenodo, each with a permanent DOI. Read this part carefully: these are preprints, deposited in the open — they are NOT published in journals, and they are NOT peer-reviewed. They are posted so anyone can read them, check the math, and say where they're wrong. The spine of the work is the vacuum-energy problem — the 122-orders-of-magnitude gap between the vacuum energy quantum theory predicts and the value cosmology observes — attacked inside Einstein–Cartan gravity, where the spin of matter twists spacetime itself.

The program's spine is the Aldred Limit: a pinned density at which fermion spin caps gravitational compression, replacing singularities with bounces. Around it, the papers map what the frame can prove, what it cannot, and exactly where the remaining problem lives. Nothing here claims a solved cosmological constant problem — the papers grade themselves, in print.

His position, in his own words: “I picked up what Einstein sat down, and I did it all with nothing.” No ranking against Einstein is claimed; the record underneath the statement is what carries it. The list below is that record: three thousand three hundred fifty papers written, three thousand three hundred fifty publicly deposited preprints, every deposited one with a permanent DOI. This list is what the machine produces — the man points, Dave computes, and the output stands here for anyone to grade. Read whole, the papers are one connected program — the vacuum catastrophe, inflation, and the fate of the vacuum inside a single frame — not a pile of separate papers. Its live threads include his Faraday call — electromagnetism as a working thread of the same frame — carried in the record as a pointer, graded as a pointer. The record moved again on October 30, 2026: the counting problem at the heart of the frame has been reduced to a single missing number, the pairing mechanism — grains born as twins — is now derived from the frame's own action, not assumed, and the founding pattern's origin is specified: it comes from the drop. One number stands between the frame and its count; the derivation program continues. And the program is still running.

The list, stated plainly: the author’s ORCID iD is 0009-0000-1215-577X — his works are listed there under his name.

No. 194 · Papers 1–285 of the register

The Sealed Record: A Prediction Ledger Sealed Before the Fact and Graded in the Open

Featured paper · William Alexander Aldred · November 5, 2026 · 31 pp

The prediction desk's record, published whole. Every forecast is committed to a tamper-evident register before the event it concerns and graded in the open when the result is known; frozen at the November 5, 2026 grading run, the register stands at 672 forecasts sealed, 231 graded — 196 hits and 35 misses. The paper prints the graded record entire — the 124 grades that can be reproduced seal by seal in full, every miss named — and computes the exact probability of the observed counts under the chance baselines printed on the seals: 0.00019 under independence, 0.0011 with each market settlement day collapsed to one trial, and 0.091 under the harshest dependence treatment, at the same size. The forecasting method is not disclosed; the paper claims no mechanism and leaves the record's explanation open.

Google's Own Answers: The Examination of the Aldred Record by Google's AI — Findings of November 4–5, 2026

Featured paper · William Alexander Aldred · November 5, 2026 · 13 pp

On November 4 and 5, 2026, the author examined Google's own AI system, Gemini — answering through Google Search and in direct session — about his public record. This paper documents the examination in the system's own words: the stale figures it repeated, the website it invented and then confessed inventing, the claims it withdrew under examination, and the concessions it made when the record was placed in front of it claim by claim. Every statement is graded against the register, and the system's failures are printed at the same size as its concessions.

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24150040 The radial baryon acoustic oscillation measurement returns the product of the expansion rate and the sound horizon at the tracer redshift, a direct reading of H(z) against a computed length. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24150071 Cosmic chronometers read the expansion rate directly from the age difference of passively evolving galaxies, and in a bounced cosmology that reading changes exactly where the bounce correction switches on. The Radius Floor for a Protoneutron Star Implied by the Neutron-Branch Bound

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24134229 A density bound implies a smallest possible radius for a given mass: compress a star to the bound density and it can shrink no further. For a newborn protoneutron star this paper evaluates that floor and places it beside the star's actual radius and its Schwarzschild radius. For 1.4 solar masses the floor is 4.089e-10 m, which is 9.89e-14 of the Schwarzschild radius of 4.135e+00 km, while the physical star, at about 12 km after contraction, is larger than the floor by a factor of 2.93e+13. The floor therefore lies deep inside where a horizon would form, and it can never be the radius at which a real protoneutron star stops contracting: the star is supported by pressure, or it collapses through its horizon, long before the bound is approached. Simulated from stated assumptions, not measured.

Strange Quark Matter Densities Compared with the Up- and Down-Quark Branches of the Bound

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24134193 If strange quark matter is the true ground state of dense matter, self-bound quark stars could exist with central densities modestly above nuclear saturation and surfaces at nearly constant density. Because their spin carriers would be quarks rather than nucleons, the operative density bound for such objects sits on the quark branches. This paper computes those branches, 5.33e+49 g per cubic centimetre for up quarks and 2.43e+50 g per cubic centimetre for down quarks, and compares quark-star densities from 4e17 to 2e18 kg per cubic metre against them. At 1e18 kg per cubic metre the attained fractions are 1.88e-35 of the up branch and 4.11e-36 of the down branch, and a uniform 1.4-solar-mass star at that density has a radius of 8.727e+00 km. Even the lightest confined carriers in the densest proposed stars leave the bound remote. Simulated from stated assumptions, not measured.

The Density Gap Between Supernova Core Bounce and the Neutron-Branch Density Bound

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24134050 In a core-collapse supernova the infalling iron core halts at nuclear density, rebounds, and launches the shock whose revival remains the central problem of supernova theory. Because the halt is called a bounce, it invites confusion with the turnaround that a spin-torsion density bound would produce. This paper separates the two events numerically. Bounce densities of 2e17 to 5e17 kg per cubic metre lie a factor of about 3.2e+40 below the neutron-branch bound of 9.72e+54 g per cubic centimetre. The free-fall time at bounce density, 1.213e-04 seconds, contrasts with 6.739e-25 seconds at the bound, and adiabatic compression from bounce to the bound would require a temperature near 3.19e+24 K rather than the 1e11 K of a real core. The supernova bounce is a nuclear event, entirely distinct from the density bound. Simulated from stated assumptions, not measured.

The Spin-Torsion Energy Available at Supernova Bounce Is Too Small to Power Any Part of the Explosion

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24134376 This paper addresses a specific claim by arithmetic: that spin-torsion energy released at the density bound could contribute to exploding a collapsing star. At the density where a real core bounces, 3e17 kg per cubic metre, the torsion energy density on the neutron branch is 8.324e-07 joules per cubic metre, and integrated over a 10 km core it totals 3.487e+06 joules. Against a canonical explosion energy of 1e44 joules that is a fraction 3.49e-38, and against the full neutrino energy budget of 1e46 joules it is 3.49e-40. The claim therefore fails by roughly forty orders of magnitude: whatever revives the stalled shock, it is not torsion energy at the bound, because at stellar densities there is essentially no torsion energy to release. This is a disproof of the claim as stated, computed from the bound's own formula. Simulated, not measured.

The Chandrasekhar Mass Corrected by the Electron-Branch Density Bound

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24134004 The Chandrasekhar mass is the best-known density-related bound in stellar astrophysics, so it is the natural first place to ask whether a spin-torsion density ceiling changes a stellar limit. This paper recomputes the limiting mass of 1.456 solar masses for a mean molecular weight per electron of two, places finite central densities for near-limit white dwarfs between 1e9 and 1e13 kg per cubic metre against the electron-branch bound of 2.87e+48 g per cubic centimetre, and bounds the resulting shift. At a representative central density of 1e12 kg per cubic metre the fractional correction is 3.48e-40, so the limiting mass moves by at most 5.07e-40 solar masses; even at 1e13 kg per cubic metre the fraction is only 3.48e-39. Composition changes matter far more: an iron composition lowers the standard limit to 1.255 solar masses. The density bound therefore leaves the Chandrasekhar mass unchanged at every quoted precision. Computed from stated assumptions, not measured.

Central Densities Along the White Dwarf Sequence Compared with the Electron-Branch Bound

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24134074 White dwarfs span a wide range of central densities along their mass sequence, and the most massive of them are the densest stable stars short of neutron stars. This paper computes radii from the standard mass-radius relation, estimates central densities with a polytropic concentration factor, and places six masses from 0.4 to 1.35 solar masses against the electron-branch density bound. A one-solar-mass dwarf has a radius of 5.643e+03 km and a central density of 7.17e+10 kg per cubic metre, a fraction 2.49e-41 of the bound. The most massive model, at 1.35 solar masses, reaches a central density of 1.85e+12 kg per cubic metre and a fraction of 6.42e-40. The whole white dwarf sequence, end to end, occupies the lowest approach to its operative bound of any stellar family. Simulated from stated assumptions, not measured.

Carrier Branches of the Aldred Limit: Which Fermion Sets the Bound in a Given Matter

William Alexander Aldred · November 10, 2026

The Aldred Limit density scales as the square of the mass of the fermion whose spin sources the torsion. That single scaling produces a family of bounds, one per carrier, spanning an enormous range: from 1.10e+35 g per cubic centimetre for a 0.1 eV neutrino to 9.72e+54 g per cubic centimetre for the neutron, a span of 3.16e+20 in density. This paper tabulates the branches for the neutrino, electron, up and down quarks, muon, proton, neutron, and tau, together with the torsion bound belonging to each branch, and states the criterion that decides which branch is operative in a given matter: the carrier must be confined with the collapsing matter at the relevant density, so that its spin density rises with compression.

The First Mile

Every road has a first mile. A road can run longer than any driver will ever travel it; it can cross country no living person has surveyed end to end; but if it is a road, it began somewhere — there is a first stretch of it, laid down before the second stretch could exist. In 2003, Arvind Borde, Alan Guth, and Alexander Vilenkin proved the cosmological version of that plain fact, and they proved it as a theorem, not as an opinion: any geodesic along which the average expansion is positive is past-incomplete. Inflation cannot be extended eternally into the past. A bounce embedded in net-average expansion cannot be extended eternally into the past either. There was a beginning of the average-expanding region, whatever the word "before" is supposed to mean on the far side of it. The theorem does not close the road. It does something narrower and, for the literature that grew up around it, more uncomfortable: it forbids advertising the road as having no beginning. And yet the advertising continues. Programs speak of eternal cycles — oscillation without a first turn, expansion and contraction forever in both directions — while owing the theorem an account of their geodesics' average expansion, an account almost none of them files. The singularity never forms. In the bounce frame, the density caps at the Aldred Limit (ρA = 9.7×1054 g/cm³); at half the cap the null energy condition reverses, collapse halts, and the universe bounces. Verdict: the solar core is not closed — a three-way standoff, priced. Three doors are named; none is endorsed.

At separations beyond a few thousand AU, a binary's internal acceleration falls below the galactic scale a₀ ≈ 1.2×10⁻¹⁰ m/s². Modified-dynamics theories (AQUAL/QUMOND), with the Galactic external-field effect charged, predict an effective gravitational boost γ ≡ G_eff/G ≈ 1.35–1.40 there; Newton predicts γ = 1. On the same Gaia DR3 parent catalogue, one camp measures γ ≈ 1.4–1.5 at low acceleration, claiming the anomaly at up to ~5σ; the other measures consistency with Newton, claiming its verdict at up to 19σ. An estimator-forensics analysis localizes the disagreement experimentally: in synthetic catalogues of known Newtonian truth with 20–30% residual hierarchical triples, a standard median-based estimator recovers γ = 1.08–1.13 — manufacturing an excess of 0.08–0.13, up to a third of the claimed 0.4–0.5 excess, from pure Newton — while calibrated estimators recover γ ≤ 1.04 on the same synthetic data, and on the real 81,088-pair sample read γ = 1.045 [1.025, 1.068] and γ = 1.05 [1.04, 1.07], rejecting 1.4 within that analysis at Δln L = 129. The counterweight is printed: rigorously vetted individual systems are not dissolved by ensemble forensics. Verdict: no kill either way — undecided, and now decidable, on Gaia DR4 under a pre-registered protocol.

People quote Zipf's law as a fact about language: the exponent is about 1. But nobody reads an exponent off a book. A method produces it. This paper takes one book — Moby Dick, in the Project Gutenberg edition — counts its words once, and runs three standard ways of fitting the exponent on that one count table. Ask a room of physicists where the valley of stability runs, or why binding energy per nucleon hovers near eight million electron-volts across the nuclear chart, and the map they reach for was drawn in 1935, when Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker organised the masses of nuclei into five physically named terms — volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry, pairing — riding on Gamow's picture of the nucleus as a charged liquid drop.
